You've heard of "tipflation" and "tip creep." But what may not be clear when you're prompted to tip your barista, hairdresser or even your mechanic is that you're often tipping on the total — tax included.
Consumer advocates, researchers say consumers find it harder to ascertain how tips are calculated these days

Cost of Living3:57Why you should do the math why you leave a tip
You've heard of "tipflation" and "tip creep."
But what may not be clear when you're prompted to tip your barista, hairdresser or even your mechanic is that you could be tipping on the total — tax included.
Back when leaving a tip meant having to do some mental or back-of-the-napkin math, the custom was to look at the subtotal before taxes and calculate from there.
But with point-of-sale terminals spitting out numbers lickety-split, it's hard to get a handle on how tipping equations are being run.

"In effect, a consumer has to take out their calculator to check if it was calculated before or after the tip, so it gets more difficult," said Sara Eve Levac, a lawyer for the Quebec-based non-profit Option Consommateurs, a consumer watchdog.

Sara Eve Levac of the Quebec-based non-profit consumer watchdog Option Consommateurs says the organization held discussion groups about tipping with consumers across Canada, and the findings were that 'people felt like it wasn't clear' if they included tax. (Maude Desbois Photographie)
In response to consumer feedback about the issue, Levac said their organization tested some restaurants and found cases where the tip was indeed calculated after the taxes.

Bonnie Simpson, a professor of consumer behaviour at Western University in London, Ont., said that in many places where we're being asked to tip these days, we often don't get itemized receipts with a clear delineation between total and subtotal.
"We get a tiny screen and it does not show us a breakdown," said Simpson, who has researched consumer attitudes toward tipping.
Sure, most sit-down restaurants still hand you a paper breakdown of everything you ordered, said Simpson, but it's straight to the point-of-sale terminal in a lot of other tipping contexts.
Even when there is a receipt that delineates the total before and after tax, it's often not obvious which is used to calculate the tip.
Levac said Option Consommateurs held discussion groups about tipping with consumers across Canada, and the findings were that "people felt like it wasn't clear."
In Quebec, new rules brought in with Bill 72 last year mean it's now against the rules for any establishment to prompt customers to tip on the tax-in total.

items: Quebec has new rules on pricing and tip calculations. Here's a breakdown

blocks.text: The Quebec government's consumer protection office told CBC in an email it has received 988 complaints and issued 389 notices since these provisions came into effect on May 7, 2025, and that the majority were for restaurants, bars and other food-related services.
It's the only province with clear rules on how tips are presented on pay machines.
Quebec moves to clamp down on growing ‘tip inflation’ at restaurants

Industry association Restaurants Canada said in a statement to CBC that it advises restaurants to "ensure automated tip suggestions on payment terminals are calculated on the pre-tax amount and presented in a clear, neutral way to ensure customers feel confident in making the best choice that reflects their experience."
Is the tech to blame?
Levac said she's read media reports in which merchants said it's difficult to change their payment terminal to calculate the tip before taxes.

But when the research team at Option Consommateurs looked at 12 common payment systems, Levac said they found it was "actually pretty easy for someone with minimal technical knowledge to be able to change the settings."

items: Tip-flation has some restaurants asking for up to 30% in tips

blocks.text: Moneris and Square are among the most used payment processors in Canada. They rent and sell the payment machines that are used by a lot of Canadian businesses.
In emails to CBC, both said their machines can be customized and it's up to businesses to decide how their tips are calculated and whether to include the tax or not.
Time for a new model?
In Edmonton, Sarah Burns said she feels privileged to be able to go out for coffees and the occasional dinner given the high cost of just about everything these days.
"But I do not like tipping on GST on my bill," she told Cost of Living.
"I would really prefer a European model where I believe servers are paid a living wage."

Western University Prof. Bonnie Simpson says tipping is a social contract we engage in as consumers and that it would take a lot of consumer pressure — and eventually legislation — to arrive at a new system. (Submitted by Bonnie Simpson)

Western University's Bonnie Simpson said tipping is a social contract we engage in as consumers and that it would take a lot of consumer pressure — and eventually legislation — to arrive at a new system.

"Somebody would need to study and propose an alternative that still allowed the hospitality industry success and still allowed the people working in it to make great wages. But it would be a huge change."
